name: Liam Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Dr Rahman. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Call me Liam, please. I'm at Northgate Family Health Centre on Station Road, and I'm usually parked by quarter to eight so I can clear some of the results inbox before the first patient. That's blood tests, scan reports, letters from the hospital, often eighty or ninety items a day. Then it's ten- to fifteen-minute appointments back to back, about thirty patients, plus phone calls and maybe one home visit at lunch.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the long game. I've known Mr Doyle for nine years, through his bypass and his wife's death, and when he walks in I can tell from his shoes whether he's coping, because when he's low he stops doing the laces. What wears me out is the paperwork: forms for insurers, sick notes, referral letters that bounce back because a box wasn't ticked. Most nights I'm typing notes at the kitchen table after Zara and Sami are in bed, and my partner Hannah says I treat the laptop like a third child.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI tools at the moment?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A bit. About a year ago Dr Okafor, our senior partner, got us a trial of one of those listening tools that writes up the consultation notes, and I use it maybe half the time. It's decent, but it once wrote that a patient had chest pain when she'd said her chest of drawers fell on her foot, so I read every word before I sign it. I'm not first in the queue for new gadgets, but once Ben, our youngest doctor, has broken one in, I'll give it a go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, but quietly, because I never got very excited either way. At the practice meeting I'd say the note-writing tool is worth keeping and the rest was a sales pitch. Online I wouldn't say anything, I don't really post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, a bit of relief and a bit of disappointment. If the machines can't take the forms off me, then the forms stay, and I'm still at the kitchen table at ten at night. The job's safe, but the bit that's slowly grinding me down is safe too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, mostly. I'd use the note tool every day instead of half the time, and I'd push Gail on reception to let it sort the repeat prescription requests, because that's the one thing it really is good at. Money-wise nothing changes: the mortgage has nineteen years left and we just keep paying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a little flat. It's like being told the extension you were saving for isn't happening, but neither is the leak in the roof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the forms grinding you down. What would that look like in five years if nothing changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now, just older. Ruth Okafor retires in two or three years and we already can't find anyone to replace her, so her patients get shared out among the rest of us. That means thirty-five patients a day instead of thirty, and less time for people like Mr Doyle, which is the part of the job I actually came for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd miss about the bigger change not happening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The idea of getting home for dinner, I suppose. Every few months someone shows us a demo that promises to give doctors their evenings back, and Hannah's started laughing when I tell her about them. In this picture she'd be right to laugh.

S0.say: I'd say I told you so, but quietly, because I never got very excited either way. The note-writing tool is worth keeping and the rest was a sales pitch.
S0.think: A bit of relief and a bit of disappointment. If the machines can't take the forms off me, the forms stay, and I'm still typing notes at the kitchen table at ten at night.
S0.do: Carries on as before and starts using the note-writing tool every day instead of half the time. Pushes reception to let it sort repeat prescription requests, and keeps paying the 19-year mortgage as normal.
S0.feel: Calm and a little flat: his job is safe, but so is the paperwork that wears him down.
S0.quote: The job's safe, but the bit that's slowly grinding me down is safe too.
S0.fieldNote: Liam's first reaction to a world without big AI change isn't relief about his job, which he never felt was at risk here, but disappointment about his evenings. The real pressure in his life is workload, made worse by a senior partner retiring with no replacement. He treats AI as a possible fix for paperwork, not as a threat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good for patients if we're careful with it. At work I'd be the one saying let's trial it on the results inbox first, with a doctor checking, before we let it near anything that touches a diagnosis. Friends would ask whether I'm getting replaced and I'd say, I'm not getting replaced, I'm getting a very fast junior doctor who never sleeps and sometimes makes things up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the clinic changes shape more than I'd admit. If the software can sort the results, write the letters and handle the simple stuff like coughs and contraception refills online, then the managers will notice they need fewer doctors per thousand patients. I don't think I'd lose my job, but I think the next doctor we'd have hired doesn't get hired, and that's young Ben's generation, not mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get properly good at the tools, not dabble. I'd do whatever short course the medical college runs, probably a weekend or two, and offer to be the doctor at Northgate who sets up how we check the AI's work, because whoever writes those rules gets a say. And I'd put a bit more aside each month, maybe a tenth more than now, just to get from four months of savings to six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a way I can manage. It's like when they brought in electronic records twenty years ago: everyone moaned for a year, then nobody could remember paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the next doctor doesn't get hired. Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ben Ashworth, our youngest. He's twenty-nine, still paying off his student loans, and he's the best of us with the computers, which is the irony. If the work that's left is the long, messy relationships, the eighty-year-olds with six conditions and a daughter who phones in crying, then he's competing with people like me who've got ten years of knowing those families.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a patient who asked whether they'd be seeing a computer instead of you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the truth: the computer will probably read their blood test before I do, but I'll still be the one who rings them. Mrs Kowalski, who's had diabetes for twenty years, already asks me whether I've 'checked with the internet', so she'd take it in her stride. It's the ones who don't trust anything new I'd need to sit with longer.

S1.say: It's good for patients if we're careful with it, so let's trial it on the results inbox first, with a doctor checking. I'm not getting replaced, I'm getting a very fast junior doctor who never sleeps and sometimes makes things up.
S1.think: The clinic changes shape more than I'd admit. I won't lose my job, but the next doctor we'd have hired doesn't get hired, and that hits Ben's generation, not mine.
S1.do: Takes a short course on clinical AI tools over a weekend or two and volunteers to set the clinic's rules for checking the AI's work. Saves about a tenth more each month to grow his savings from four to six months of expenses.
S1.feel: Uneasy but in control. He compares it to the move to electronic records: a year of complaints, then nobody remembers paper.
S1.quote: I'm not getting replaced, I'm getting a very fast junior doctor who never sleeps and sometimes makes things up.
S1.fieldNote: Liam's public and private views differ mainly in who he thinks pays the price. In public he says nobody gets replaced; in private he expects fewer new doctors to be hired and worries for his younger colleague Ben. His instinct is to get close to the rules for checking the AI, on the idea that whoever writes those rules keeps some control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need rules before we need anything else, like who's responsible when the machine gets it wrong. I'd probably sign whatever letter the doctors' association sent round. To friends I'd say patients will still want a person in the room, and I'd believe about half of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it's really better than me at diagnosis, and cheaper, then I'm a forty-three-year-old with a mortgage and a skill that just lost most of its price. The part that's left is holding someone's hand while they get bad news, and I'm not sure anyone pays a doctor's wage for that. Two years is nothing. It took us three years just to agree on a new phone system at Northgate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first thing is money, because two years doesn't leave time for anything clever. We'd stop the plan for the loft conversion, cancel the summer trip to Hannah's sister, and put everything we can into savings. Hannah teaches chemistry, so I'd want to know if her job looks safer than mine, because if it does, she becomes the steady income and I become whatever comes next. I'd talk to the bank early about stretching the mortgage before everyone else is in the same queue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor's gone soft. Not panic yet, but I'd be the one lying awake doing sums at three in the morning while Hannah sleeps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Zara and Sami?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, at first. Zara's eleven and she wants to be a vet, and I'd hate to be the dad who tells her that's pointless before anyone actually knows. I'd probably say the world's changing fast and we'll work it out together, which is what my own father said when his shop closed, and I remember not believing him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the first thing is money. If your pay stopped, what gets cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sami's swimming club and the second car go first, then the eating out, which is already only once a month. The thing I wouldn't cut is the kids' school and the house, because moving them would feel like admitting defeat. With four months of savings, we'd have until about the start of the next school year before the mortgage got scary.

S2.say: We need rules before we need anything else, like who's responsible when the machine gets it wrong. Patients will still want a person in the room, and I'd believe about half of that.
S2.think: If it's better than me at diagnosis and cheaper, I'm a forty-three-year-old with a mortgage and a skill that just lost most of its price. Two years is nothing when the clinic took three years to agree on a phone system.
S2.do: Stops the loft conversion, cancels the summer trip and puts everything spare into savings. Asks the bank early about stretching the mortgage, and works out with Hannah whether her teaching job should become the family's main income.
S2.feel: Like the floor has gone soft: not panic yet, but awake at three in the morning doing sums.
S2.quote: Two years is nothing. It took us three years just to agree on a new phone system at Northgate.
S2.fieldNote: With only two years of warning, Liam has no plan beyond defence: cut spending, save, and talk to the bank before the queue forms. His public line that patients will want a person is one he admits he only half believes. The strongest moment was about his father's shop closing, which shapes how he would and wouldn't talk to his children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty much what I said with the fast one, but calmer, and I'd add that we have time to do this properly. At the practice meeting I'd want us to decide now which parts of the job we'd hand over and which we'd fight to keep. Online, still nothing, though I might finally join one of those doctors' forums just to read what people are planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is a real number. It's enough time to get ready, but not enough to wait and see. I'd be forty-eight, the mortgage would still have fourteen years on it, and Zara would be starting university. And I know myself: I like to let someone else try things first, and in this picture that habit could cost me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd overpay the mortgage every month for those five years, even a small amount, so the number's lower when it lands. I'd move my work towards the parts a machine is least likely to take: I'd ask Ruth whether I could take over her home visits and her palliative patients, meaning people who are dying and need comfort more than cures, and do a diploma in palliative care in the evenings. I'd also get very good at the AI tools in the meantime, because the doctor who can run them will last longer than the doctor who can't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's a busy kind of anxious. Having a list helps me, even when I'm not sure the list is right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it would be Zara's first year at university. Would that change anything for her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would change the conversations. If she still wants to be a vet, I'd ask her to think about which part of the job is about the animal and which part is about the frightened owner, because I'd bet on the second part lasting longer. I wouldn't tell her what to study, but I'd stop saying 'any degree is a good degree,' because I don't think I'd believe it anymore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you like to let someone else try things first. Is that what you'd do here, or not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd catch myself doing it. In year one I'd still be saying let's wait for the evidence, because that's how doctors are trained. Maybe by year two I'd look at Ben, who'd have already moved on to something new, and realise the evidence was him.

S3.say: We have time to do this properly. At the practice we should decide now which parts of the job we hand over and which we fight to keep.
S3.think: Five years is enough time to get ready, but not enough to wait and see. I'd be forty-eight with fourteen years left on the mortgage, and my habit of letting others go first could cost me.
S3.do: Overpays the mortgage every month for five years and asks to take over the senior partner's home visits and palliative patients. Starts an evening diploma in palliative care and gets fluent in the AI tools in the meantime.
S3.feel: Anxious, but a busy kind of anxious; having a list helps even when he isn't sure the list is right.
S3.quote: Five years is a real number. It's enough time to get ready, but not enough to wait and see.
S3.fieldNote: Five years of warning turns Liam from defensive to planning: overpaying the mortgage, moving towards palliative care and home visits, and rethinking advice to his daughter. He's frank that his usual habit of waiting for proof is the danger here. He sees the human, emotional side of medicine as the part most likely to last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and we'd be fools to waste it. At work I'd argue for the practice to start training people now, the nurses and the reception staff as well as the doctors. Like I said with the five-year one, I'd want us to decide what we keep before someone decides for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is the dangerous one, because I'd waste the first five. I'd tell myself there's plenty of time, the evidence isn't in, Ruth will retire and things will settle. Then I'd look up at fifty and be in the same spot as the two-year picture, only older.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make myself a rule: one concrete step a year, written on the calendar in January. Year one, the palliative care diploma; year two, start overpaying the mortgage so it's paid off by around fifty-five instead of sixty-two. I'd also talk to Hannah about whether one of us retrains properly, maybe her moving into school leadership, because two incomes in two different kinds of work feels safer than two in jobs that might fall at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly uneasy rather than scared. It's further off, and I'd be fifty-three when it lands, which is old enough to have a plan and young enough to still need an income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be fifty-three. Does the timing feel better or worse than for, say, Ben or Ruth?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth's lucky, she'll be retired before any of it, gardening and complaining about her knees. Ben is thirty-nine by then, still young enough to start something completely new. I'm in the awkward middle, too young to stop and a bit too settled to start from scratch, so I'd have to be the one who makes himself move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would get you to actually take that first step, rather than waiting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing it in my own clinic, probably. If the AI started catching things in the results inbox that I'd missed, not once but every week, that would do it. I remember the first time the computer flagged a drug interaction I'd overlooked, years ago, and I went home and checked my prescribing for a month.

S4.say: Ten years is a gift, and we'd be fools to waste it. The practice should start training everyone now, nurses and reception staff as well as doctors.
S4.think: Ten years is the dangerous one, because I'd waste the first five telling myself there's plenty of time. Then I'd look up at fifty and be in the same spot as the two-year picture, only older.
S4.do: Sets himself one concrete step a year, starting with the palliative care diploma, then overpays the mortgage to clear it by about 55 instead of 62. Talks with Hannah about her moving into school leadership so their two incomes don't depend on jobs that might fall at once.
S4.feel: Mostly uneasy rather than scared, knowing he'd be 53 when it lands: old enough to plan, young enough to still need an income.
S4.quote: Ten years is the dangerous one, because I'd waste the first five.
S4.fieldNote: The most surprising answer of the interview: Liam sees the longest warning as the riskiest for him, because it feeds his habit of waiting for proof. His fix is a rule of one step a year, written on the calendar. He places himself in an awkward middle between a colleague who will retire first and a younger one who can start again, and says only seeing the AI beat him in his own clinic would truly move him.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028, because there's no time to do anything except cut back and hope. What would help is something like a bridge: a guaranteed income for a couple of years for people with mortgages and kids, and a fast, paid route into the parts of care that still need a person, like palliative care or looking after old people at home. And honestly, clear rules on who's responsible when the machine's wrong, so doctors aren't just there to take the blame.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the patients. Mr Doyle doesn't come in because his heart tablets need adjusting; he comes in because it's the only conversation he has all week. Whatever happens to me, I'd want someone to be paid to have that conversation with him, even if the tablets are sorted by a machine.

headlineQuote: Mr Doyle doesn't come in because his heart tablets need adjusting; he comes in because it's the only conversation he has all week.
portrait: Liam Rahman is a 43-year-old family doctor at a busy local clinic, with a partner who teaches chemistry, two school-age children, a mortgage and about four months of savings. He's practical, middle-of-the-road and willing to change once something is proven, and he already uses an AI note-writing tool about half the time. If AI stalls, he's mostly sorry the paperwork stays; with strong but steady change he plans to master the tools and help write the clinic's rules for checking them. Facing full AGI, the warning time shapes everything: two years means cutting back and saving, five means overpaying the mortgage and moving towards palliative care, and ten worries him in a different way because he fears he'd waste the first five years waiting for proof.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because two years leaves no time to do anything except cut back and hope.
whatWouldHelp: A guaranteed income for a couple of years for people with mortgages and children, plus a fast, paid route into care work that still needs a person, such as palliative care. He also wants clear rules on who's responsible when the AI is wrong, so doctors aren't just there to take the blame.
